description: We are a 3 student team from Turkey, aiming to become Earth Trend Detectives!
summary: Metalimnion is a visual analysis app which simplifies the viewing and observation of lakes worldwide and significant changes that have affected said lakes. Metalimnion is a sophisticated app that can display individual measurements of area and surface temperature over the years and analyze these measurements to attribute changes to climatological phenomena or human activity. The analyses are then evaluated on the basis of reliability using statistical techniques and are summarized. All analyzed lakes are shown on the various available easy-to-navigate maps with helpful circles and name descriptors. It addresses the challenge by making significant changes regarding lakes much easier to view and reason about, especially for non-experts. It allows everyone to see the change and future predictions concerning water area and surface temperature allowing them to act against the day by day shrinking of water resources, which are already very limited. This matters because global water trends affect many living things worldwide, and more attention must be drawn to crucial concerns such as this if we, the people, want to tend to our planet well.
details:
What does it do?

Metalimnion turns 40 years of NASA/USGS Landsat data into a free web map that shows which of the world's lakes are shrinking, when the change began, where it is heading, and how much of it is climate versus human water use. It gives residents, farmers, journalists and water managers an early warning and a factual basis to act while there is still water left to save.

How does it work?

Metalimnion shows how the world's lakes are changing and why, on one interactive world map. Every analyzed lake is a circle sized by its area and coloured by its trend: shrinking, growing or stable.

Clicking a lake opens its full record:

  • Water surface area for every year from 1985 to 2025, and surface temperature.
  • The trend, with a statistical test of whether the change is real and how fast it is.
  • The emergence year: when the lake left its normal range for good.
  • A forecast of the coming years, based on the trend.
  • The cause: how much of the loss rain and evaporation can explain, and how much points to other causes such as irrigation and water withdrawal.
  • A reliability rating and a one-paragraph plain-language summary, in English and Turkish.

Lakes can be compared side by side, and any other lake can be looked up and analyzed on demand. 17 lakes are pre-analyzed, including the Aral Sea, Lake Urmia, Lake Chad, the Dead Sea, Great Salt Lake, Lake Mead, Lake Poopo, Lake Titicaca, and Turkey's Burdur, Tuz, Van, Egirdir and Aksehir lakes.

What benefits does it have?

  • Readable in seconds. 40 years of satellite data become one picture anyone can read. No remote-sensing skills, software or downloads are needed.
  • It answers "why", not only "what". It separates climate from human use, which is the question that decides what action is possible.
  • Honest about uncertainty. Every result carries a reliability rating. When the data are too weak, the app shows no number instead of a misleading one.
  • Global and comparable. The same method for every lake makes it easy to see which lakes are in the most danger.
  • Free and open. Open data, open-source code (MIT), no account

Impact

Turkey has already lost a lake. Lake Akşehir, on the border of Konya and Afyonkarahisar, covered about 290 km² in the late 1980s. In Metalimnion’s late-summer 2025 measurement its water area is 0 km². News reports tell the same story on the ground: fishing once fed the surrounding villages, and unregulated agricultural irrigation together with climate change is blamed for the lake drying out completely.

Akşehir is a warning, not an exception. In the same region, Lake Burdur has lost 42% of its 1985–1990 area and Lake Eğirdir 11%. If the past trend continues, Burdur loses about another quarter of today’s surface by 2040.

The world is losing more every year. The Southern Aral Sea is down 90%, Lake Mead 49%, Lake Urmia 47% and Great Salt Lake 38% in our records. On the current path, Lake Mead and Lake Urmia would each lose more than half of what remains by 2040. Across nearly 2,000 of the biggest lakes and reservoirs, a little over half shrank between 1992 and 2020, and about a quarter of humanity lives in the basin of a lake that is drying.

The loss is noticed too late. What follows is always the same: lost drinking and irrigation water, collapsed fisheries, salt and dust storms, displaced communities and lost habitat. The evidence was in satellite archives for decades, but the people living beside these lakes could not read it.

Metalimnion makes the next Akşehir visible before it happens. For any lake it shows when the change began, how fast it is going, where the current path leads, and whether the cause is mainly climate or mainly human use. That last answer matters most: a lake shrinking from withdrawal can still be saved by local decisions on irrigation and allocation. It is free, open, in Turkish and English, and works for 1,314 indexed lakes, so no community has to wait for experts to choose its lake.

What do we hope to achieve?

  • Make lake loss visible and understandable to everyone, not only to experts.
  • Give people and local decision makers the evidence to act early, before limited water resources shrink further.
  • Draw more public attention to global water trends, which affect people and wildlife worldwide.
  • Grow from 17 lakes to all major lakes and reservoirs, add more languages, and add water level and volume from newer satellite missions.
  • Add alerts when a lake crosses a critical level.
  • Bring it into schools as a hands-on way to teach climate and water science with real NASA data.

The Pipeline:

  1. Collect: For each lake, late-summer Landsat 4-5 and 8-9 scenesfrom 1985 to 2025 are read from the cloud.
  2. Measure: A water index (MNDWI) separates water from land in every scene, giving the lake outline and its area for each year. The Landsat thermal band gives surface temperature over pure-water pixels.
  3. Test the trend: The Mann-Kendall test and the Sen slope show whether a change is statistically real and how fast it is.
  4. Find the turning point: The first years define the lake's normal range. The emergence year is when the lake left that range for good.
  5. Explain the cause: Precipitation and evaporation over the lake's catchment are compared with the area change. This estimates the share climate can explain; the rest points to other causes.
  6. Rate and forecast: Every lake gets a reliability rating and a trend-based forecast. When the data are too weak, the app shows no number.
  7. Summarize: The numbers become a short plain-language summary, and a glossary explains each technical word.
  8. Show: Results appear on the map with NASA GIBS imagery or vector basemaps, with charts, a comparison table and live cards of the latest conditions.

Technical Details

Every number in the app comes from a documented, reproducible method with fixed parameters, all in the open-source code(github.com/Saybrone/Metalimnion).

  • API: A FastAPI service exposes the lake list, full lake records, forecasts (horizon 2026-2060), yearly water masks as PNG, live cards, lake lookup by coordinate, side-by-side comparison of up to 6 lakes, and on-demand analysis jobs.
  • On-demand analysis: The map carries an index of 1,314 lakes from Natural Earth. A request (up to 20,000 km²) enters a SQLite job queue with at most 2 analyses running at once. Every 5th year is processed first for a quick preliminary picture, then the gaps are filled, with live progress. Results are marked unverified.
  • Live cards: Latest Landsat area and temperature versus the same 45-day window a year earlier, and water-year precipitation versus the 1991-2020 normal. Each source is cached for 3 hours and fails independently; a failed refresh serves the last good value marked stale.
  • Deployment: One Docker image, deployed on Render's free plan with a health check and auto-deploy on commit.
  • Easily Deployable: Anyone can deploy it in their machines and use our software
  • Offline mode: Pre-computed lakes, stored water masks, a Natural Earth basemap and stored satellite snapshots keep the app usable without internet.

Tech Stack

  • Languages: Python, TypeScript, HTML/CSS
  • Frontend: FastAPI and Uvicorn
  • Backend: React, Vite, MapLibre GL (maps), Apache ECharts (charts)
  • Deployment and tooling:Docker, Render, Git and GitHub

Math Behind it

  • Water: MNDWI = (Green − SWIR1) / (Green + SWIR1); water if > 0. Area = water pixels × pixel size².
  • Trend: Sen slope = median of (Aⱼ − Aᵢ) / (tⱼ − tᵢ), tested with Mann-Kendall.
  • Emergence year: first year the trend line stays more than 2σ from the mean of the first 12 years.
  • Climate share: fit ΔA = a·n + b·Σ(P − E) on 1985–1999; share = predicted loss / observed loss after 1999.
  • Reliability: “low” if 20% or more of years jump by over 15% of the 1985–1990 mean area.
  • Forecast: trend + AR(1) noise, used only if it beats “no change” by more than 5% in backtests.

How is your project creative?

Most lake tools stop at showing that a lake is shrinking. Metalimnion goes on to ask why: it estimates how much of the loss rain and evaporation can explain and how much points to human use, which is the answer that decides what action is possible. It also treats honesty as a design feature. Every result carries a reliability rating, and when the data are too weak the app shows no number at all instead of a misleading one. Finally, it turns 40 years of raw satellite scenes into one plain-language paragraph in English and Turkish, so a farmer can read the same evidence as a scientist.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Audience: residents, farmers, journalists and local officials, not only experts.
  • Scientific honesty: tested trends, uncertainty intervals and clear limits. The unexplained share is a sign of human impact, not proof.
  • Comparability: one method and fixed parameters for every lake, so lakes can be ranked fairly.
  • Cost and access: only free, open data and a free 512 MB server, with no login, so any school or municipality can run it.
  • Risk of misuse: forecasts are labelled as extrapolations, not predictions, so results are not read as blame or certainty.
  • Local relevance: Turkish lakes such as Akşehir, Burdur and Eğirdir sit beside global cases like the Aral Sea and Lake Urmia.
